units.text: nikpak is a command-line archiver for the .nik format. It was designed around four ideas: compress better than the established tools, do it faster, protect data with modern cryptography, and run unchanged on Windows, macOS and Linux as a single small executable.

units.text: nikpak is aimed at people who archive large amounts of media or source code and care about size and speed, at developers who want a scriptable archiver with sane exit codes and a documented format, and at anyone who needs strong encryption without trusting a closed implementation. Because the command line follows RAR conventions, front-ends such as Total Commander can drive it with little or no reconfiguration.

units.text: Chapters 2 and 3 describe what nikpak does and how to use it. Chapters 4 to 7 explain the architecture, the file format, the compression engine and the media codecs. units.text: Hindi, Bengali and Arabic need shaping: letters change form and join, vowel signs move around their consonant, and Arabic runs right to left. egui draws one glyph per character, which would print these languages wrongly, so nikpak orders such texts with the Unicode bidirectional algorithm (unicode-bidi), shapes them with rustybuzz (a Rust port of HarfBuzz), rasterises them with ab_glyph and paints the result as an image (textshape.rs). Latin words and numbers inside them keep the Inter font. Long translations are reduced to fit their buttons, and boxes grow with their text. The translations (i18n.rs) were written with machine assistance; a review by native speakers is welcome.

units.text: nikpak is a single Rust program of about 9,600 lines (including its unit tests) in sixteen source files, plus the private licence tool nikpak-keygen. Its central design rule is streaming: files are read in 256 KiB pieces, pushed through a chain of writers, and never held in memory as a whole (the only exceptions are BMP pixel data, which is limited to 256 MiB, and the 64 KiB working buffers of the codecs).

units.text: Compressing all files as one stream lets the compressor find repetitions between files, which matters enormously for source trees and document collections (the benchmark in chapter 11 shows RAR's non-solid output being almost twice as large as its solid output on 10,949 files). The price is sequential access: extracting a single file requires decompressing what precedes it. nikpak reduces the cost of this for media entries by skipping over them without decoding.

units.text: Zstandard combines LZ77 matching with an entropy stage built from Huffman coding and finite-state entropy (FSE). Compared with the Deflate algorithm of ZIP it finds matches over a far larger window, models literals and match lengths with tighter entropy codes, and decodes at gigabytes per second. It is also an open, widely audited format, which keeps nikpak's data recoverable by independent tools.

Zstandard

coding and finite-state entropy (FSE). Compared with the Deflate
algorithm of ZIP it finds matches over a far larger window, models
literals and match lengths with tighter entropy codes, and decodes at
gigabytes per second. It is also an open, widely audited format,

units.text: At Zstandard level 15 and above nikpak enables a 2^27 byte (128 MiB) match window and long-distance matching. Source trees, document sets and backups contain many near-duplicate files that lie far apart in the stream; a normal 8 MiB window cannot see across them. On the 197 MB test set this reduced the output at -m5 from 26.3 MB to 24.4 MB and at -m4 from 29.5 MB to 26.8 MB, at no cost in speed for -m4 and a small one for -m5. A window of 2^27 is within Zstandard's default decoder limit, so any standard decoder can read the data.

units.text: A general-purpose compressor sees bytes. It does not know that a WAV file is a waveform whose next sample is predictable from the previous ones, or that neighbouring pixels of a photograph are nearly equal. nikpak's media layer supplies that knowledge: it recognises such files, applies a lossless transform that exposes the redundancy, and lets the compressor (or a dedicated codec) exploit it. This is where nikpak gains most against RAR.

units.text: Writing an archive is the only chance to detect an encoder bug, so the NAC encoder does not trust itself. After encoding each block it decodes the block again and compares the result with the original samples. On any difference it re-encodes the block as verbatim (which cannot fail) and checks again; if even that fails, archiving stops with an explicit error and the suggestion to use -mc-. The fallback path is exercised by the unit tests, which force verbatim coding for every combination of bit depth and channel count, and the mechanism turns a possible silent data-loss bug into a detected, recoverable condition.

units.text: Shuffle separates the bytes of the samples into planes: all least-significant bytes of channel 0, then all most-significant bytes of channel 0, then channel 1, and so on, in blocks of 32768 frames. units.text: Modern office files are ZIP archives of XML (docx, xlsx, pptx, odt, ods), and PDF files store their pages in Deflate (FlateDecode) streams. Their content is therefore already compressed, and no archiver can shrink it much: in the 1.1 benchmark, 6.6 MB of .xlsx files only went down to 5.6 MB with 7-Zip. nikpak 1.2 removes that obstacle.

units.text: On the office set of section 11.7 this is what makes nikpak smaller than every other archiver. The 6.6 MB of .xlsx files contain 71 MB of XML once decoded, and that XML compresses far better than Deflate did. The cost is time: preflate analyses roughly 15 MB of plain data per second. For that reason recompression is used at -m4 and -m5 only, where it pays off (measured: -m3 gained 0.5 % for six times the time). Limits: files up to 512 MiB, and per stream up to 512 MiB of plain data and 64 MiB of corrections. -mc- turns it off.

units.text: The bulk data is protected with XChaCha20-Poly1305, an authenticated-encryption-with-associated-data (AEAD) cipher: ChaCha20 provides a 256-bit-key stream cipher, the X variant extends its nonce to 192 bits (large enough to choose at random without ever repeating), and Poly1305 adds a 128-bit authentication tag to every sealed message. units.text: A frequently cited quantum threat is that an adversary records encrypted data today and decrypts it when a quantum computer exists. For systems that exchange keys with RSA or elliptic curves, such as TLS connections or e-mail encryption, this is real. A nikpak archive has no key exchange: its key comes from a secret that never leaves the user's head or password manager. A stored copy can only be opened later by guessing that secret, and quantum computers do not make that fundamentally easier.

units.text: Both nikpak and RAR5 encrypt with a 256-bit symmetric key, so both are untouched by Shor's algorithm and both keep about 128 bits of security against Grover's. Neither claim distinguishes them. What nikpak adds on top is a memory-hard password step (which makes the dominant real-world attack, password guessing, far more expensive) and authenticated encryption (which makes tampering detectable). It has also been designed from the start on the assumption that no public-key primitive will ever be part of the archive format, and its roadmap commits to a hybrid post-quantum scheme if public-key sharing is added.

units.text: The test campaign is the reason several defects do not exist in the released program. Two examples: a Rice-parameter search that failed for 32-bit audio and would have written a multi-gigabyte code (found by the unit test matrix and fixed), and a zstd checksum failure that was reported with the generic exit code 2 instead of 3 (found in the tamper tests and fixed). A third example is the benchmark methodology itself: the first comparison with RAR used its non-solid default, which flattered nikpak on source code; it was redone in solid mode, and the results in chapter 11 are the corrected ones.

test campaign is the reason several defects do not exist in the

by the unit test matrix and fixed), and a zstd checksum failure that
was reported with the generic exit code 2 instead of 3 (found in the
tamper tests and fixed). A third example is the benchmark methodology
itself: the first comparison with RAR used its non-solid default,
which flattered nikpak on source code; it was redone in solid mode,

A general-purpose compressor sees bytes..html:

legitimate user is a fraction of a second, paid once per archive.

A frequently cited quantum threat is tha.html:
A
frequently cited quantum threat is that an adversary records
encrypted data today and decrypts it when a quantum computer exists.
For systems that exchange keys with RSA or elliptic curves, such as
TLS connections or e-mail encryption, this is real. A nikpak archive
has no key exchange: its key comes from a secret that never leaves
the user's head or password manager. A stored copy can only be opened
later by guessing that secret, and quantum computers do not make that
fundamentally easier.

Both nikpak and RAR5 encrypt with a 256-.html:
Both
nikpak and RAR5 encrypt with a 256-bit symmetric key, so both are
untouched by Shor's algorithm and both keep about 128 bits of
security against Grover's. Neither claim distinguishes them. What
nikpak adds on top is a memory-hard password step (which makes the
dominant real-world attack, password guessing, far more expensive)
and authenticated encryption (which makes tampering detectable). It
has also been designed from the start on the assumption that no
public-key primitive will ever be part of the archive format, and its
roadmap commits to a hybrid post-quantum scheme if public-key sharing
is added.

				and --extract-here / --extract-to under a virtual display;
				encrypted archives ask for their password and extract identical
				files; every new interface text is translated in the ten
				languages (the every-language-translates-every-text assertion).

Interactive

	wrong passwords on opening.

Tampering, truncation, chunk reordering,.html:
Tampering,
truncation, chunk reordering, header manipulation, garbage files and
the path-traversal archives of section 10.1 were run against every
release candidate. The results are tabulated in sections 8.6 and
10.1; the expected outcome in every case is a refusal, a clear
message and a non-zero exit code, never a panic and never a write
outside the destination.

The test campaign is the reason several.html:
The
test campaign is the reason several defects do not exist in the
released program. Two examples: a Rice-parameter search that failed
for 32-bit audio and would have written a multi-gigabyte code (found
by the unit test matrix and fixed), and a zstd checksum failure that
was reported with the generic exit code 2 instead of 3 (found in the
tamper tests and fixed). A third example is the benchmark methodology
itself: the first comparison with RAR used its non-solid default,
which flattered nikpak on source code; it was redone in solid mode,
and the results in chapter 11 are the corrected ones.

The format is one solid stream. Deleting.html: The format is one solid stream. Deleting (nikpak d, or Delete in unNik) writes the archive again; adding files to an existing archive is not supported: create a new archive, or overwrite with -o+..

Integer
				PCM WAV and AIFF, ProTracker MOD, uncompressed BMP. Float WAV,

				compression.
